title: Introduction
text:
Objectives
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:

Define core machine learning concepts and learning types.
Identify features, targets, models, and algorithms.
Explain generalization and bias–variance trade-offs.
Apply the basic machine learning workflow using scikit-learn.

These notes follow the slides in order, grouped into the four parts of the course outline: introduction to machine learning, features and models, the bias–variance trade-off, and the machine learning workflow.

title: Introduction
text:
What is machine learning?
Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence where computers learn patterns from data and make predictions without being explicitly programmed.
It helps to break a machine learning system into three parts:








Part
What it is
Example




Input
Historical data
Spreadsheets, sensor readings, images, text


Process
A learning algorithm
Linear regression, decision trees, a neural network


Output
A predictive model
A trained function that makes predictions on new input data



Machine learning draws on computer science, artificial intelligence, statistics, and mathematics. The combination matters: statistics supplies the reasoning about uncertainty, and computer science supplies the means to apply that reasoning to data at scale. [CHECK — this gloss on why the combination matters is mine; the slide lists the fields but does not characterise their roles.]

title: Introduction
text:
Machine learning vs. traditional programming
The difference is in what you supply and what the computer produces.




You supply
Computer produces




Traditional programming
Rules + data
Answers


Machine learning
Data + answers
Rules (the model)



A spam filter makes the contrast concrete. In traditional programming you write the rule yourself — this fragment assumes subject holds the email’s subject line:
if "FREE!!!" in subject:
    label = "spam"
In machine learning you supply 10,000 labeled emails, and the algorithm produces the rule. That rule is the model.
Machine learning is the tool for problems where the rules are too complex, unknown, or constantly changing to write by hand. Spam is a good example of all three at once: the patterns are subtle, nobody can enumerate them, and senders deliberately change tactics. [CHECK — the “all three at once” reading of the spam example is my elaboration; the slide states the three conditions but does not tie them to spam.]

title: Introduction
section: Where machine learning fits in AI
text:
Where machine learning fits in AI
The terms nest inside one another:
Artificial Intelligence → Machine Learning (this course) → Deep Learning → LLMs
Artificial intelligence is the broad goal of getting systems to perform tasks that normally require human cognition and decision-making. Machine learning is the subset that learns those capabilities from data.
Some parts of AI are not machine learning: knowledge representation, constraint optimization, logical and probabilistic reasoning, and planning. These solve problems by reasoning over rules you provide rather than by learning patterns from examples. [CHECK — this contrast is mine; the slide notes name these areas but do not say how they work.]
ChatGPT is one member of this family. This course teaches the family — the concepts every member shares.

title: Introduction
text:
What is a model?
A model is a mathematical function that maps inputs to outputs to make predictions:
\[\hat{y} = f_{\theta}(x)\]
For a linear model:
\[f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\]
where:

\(x\) is the input feature
\(\hat{y}\) is the predicted output
\(\theta\) are the model parameters — the values the model learns during training

The parameters are what training produces. Once trained, the model can be reused over and over to predict outcomes.

A worked example
Suppose training on rideshare data produced \(\theta_0 = 2.50\) and \(\theta_1 = 1.75\), where \(x\) is trip distance in miles. The fitted model is
\[\hat{y} = 2.50 + 1.75x\]
For a 3.2-mile trip:
\[\hat{y} = 2.50 + 1.75(3.2) = 2.50 + 5.60 = 8.10\]
so the model predicts $8.10. Read the parameters this way: \(\theta_0\) is the base fare that applies to any trip, and \(\theta_1\) is the additional cost per mile.
[CHECK — the numbers 2.50 and 1.75, the 3.2-mile trip, the resulting $8.10, and the reading of \(\theta_0\) as a base fare and \(\theta_1\) as cost per mile are all mine. The slides give the formula and the rideshare setting but no fitted values and no interpretation of the coefficients.]

title: Introduction
text:
What is an algorithm?
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure used to train a model on data.
\[\mathcal{A} : (\textit{data},\ \textit{hyperparameters}) \rightarrow f_{\theta^{*}}\]
It takes:

Input: training data and hyperparameters
Process: optimization rules
Output: a trained model \(f_{\theta^{*}}\), where \(\theta^{*}\) are the best-fitting parameters

Gradient descent algorithms are used to train regression models. In scikit-learn, SGDRegressor() uses stochastic gradient descent, updating the model’s weights gradually as it sees each data point.

title: Introduction
text:
Model vs. algorithm
This distinction is subtle but really important:

A model is the mathematical function that makes predictions. Once trained, it can be reused over and over.
An algorithm is the method used to train the model. It iteratively adjusts the model’s parameters to reduce error.

Put another way: the model is the structure, and the algorithm is the recipe for filling in that structure with the right values. The algorithm is the process; the model is the result.
The two terms are sometimes used interchangeably in casual conversation, but the difference matters once you start talking about training, optimization, and deployment.

title: Introduction
section: Worked example: predicting a rideshare price
text:
Worked example: predicting a rideshare price
The goal is to predict the price of a ride using input features.
For each trip, a rideshare company records inputs such as distance, starting location, traffic conditions, time of day, and vehicle type. Those inputs are passed into a machine learning model, which uses an algorithm or statistical model to predict the price. The predicted price is the model’s output.
This is a supervised learning task: the training data is labeled, because the correct price of each past trip is already known. Once trained, the model can predict the price of a new trip from similar features.

A dataset is a structured collection of data, consisting of:

Features (or variables): a measurable property — a column. For example time, price, or vehicle type.
Instances (or samples): a single data point — a row. For example one rideshare trip.

title: Introduction
text:
Input and output features
Features split into two roles:

Input features (predictors, explanatory variables, \(\mathbf{X}\)): the known information fed into the model.
Output feature (target, response, \(\mathbf{y}\)): the value we want the model to predict.

In the rideshare example, the input is distance and the output is price:

input feature: distance → model → output feature: price

A useful shorthand: inputs are what you know, and the output is what you want to find out. Which features play which role is decided by the machine learning task, or research question. Choosing good input features is critical to building accurate models.

title: Introduction
text:
Types of machine learning
The type of machine learning you use depends on the task and on what data you have.








Type
Data
Typical tasks




Supervised
Data has labels
Regression (predict a number), classification (predict a category)


Unsupervised
No labels: find structure
Clustering (group similar rows), dimension reduction (compress columns)


Reinforcement
Learn from rewards
—



Applied to the rideshare setting:

Predicting the price of a trip from distance and time is supervised, since the output feature (price) is known.
Categorizing customers as “commuters”, “sports fans”, or “tourists” is unsupervised, since those categories are not an observed feature.
Adjusting the price after a customer declines is reinforcement learning: the prediction is updated based on the customer’s decision.

Two further paradigms — semi-supervised and self-supervised learning — are covered below.

title: Introduction
text:
Supervised learning
Models learn from labeled data: we give them both the inputs and the correct outputs, and the model learns the relationship between the two. It is the most common machine learning approach.
There are two categories:

Regression predicts numbers. Example: predict a ride price, such as $17.32.
Classification predicts categories. Example: predict animal type, cat vs. dog.

The quick test: if the output is numeric, it is regression; if it is categorical, it is classification.

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised learning
Models find structure in unlabeled data — no output labels are provided. The model is given a dataset and asked to discover structure or relationships within it.

Clustering: group rides into “commuters”, “sports fans”, “tourists”.
Outlier detection: find suspicious rides with abnormally high prices.
Dimensionality reduction: transform the data, for example with PCA — combining time and distance into a single “trip intensity” measure.

This is especially useful for exploratory analysis, or whenever labels are unavailable.

title: Introduction
text:
Reinforcement learning
Models learn by trial and error: they take actions and receive feedback. A model — called an agent — interacts with an environment and learns from the rewards or penalties it receives.

Agent: the decision-maker
Environment: where it operates
Reward: feedback after an action

A self-driving car learning to stay in its lane earns rewards when it stays centered and penalties when it crosses a lane. Reinforcement learning is used in robotics, game AI, and recommendation systems.

title: Introduction
text:
Semi-supervised learning
Semi-supervised learning combines a small amount of labeled data with a large pool of unlabeled data.
The motivation is cost: labeling data is time-consuming and expensive, so you will often have plenty of unlabeled instances and few labeled ones. Some algorithms can work with data that is only partially labeled.
For example, only 100 rides have prices labeled, but 10,000 do not. The model starts with the labeled data, then generalizes by learning from the rest. This is widely used in domains like medical imaging and natural language processing, where labeled data is rare but unlabeled data is abundant.

title: Introduction
text:
Self-supervised learning
Self-supervised learning learns from unlabeled data by creating its own labels. No human labeling is involved — the labels are generated from the input itself.

In NLP: mask a word in a sentence and train the model to guess it. Given “The cab arrived at the ___“, the model learns to predict the missing word from the surrounding context.
In vision: cut out part of an image and train the model to predict what is missing.

This approach is behind large language models such as ChatGPT, BERT, and DALL·E. Its power is that it can learn from vast amounts of raw data without manual annotation.

text:

Prescribing a new chemotherapy drug dosage based on a patient’s response to earlier treatment.
Predicting whether a nurse is likely to quit.
Grouping patients with similar clinical profiles from EHRs, with no outcome labels.
Pretraining a model on clinical notes by predicting masked words.
Training a diagnosis model with 100 labeled X-rays and 10,000 unlabeled ones.

[CHECK — this reasoning guidance is mine.] Two questions resolve most cases. First: are there labels, none, or only a few? Second: does the model receive feedback on its own actions over time, or does it generate its own labels from the raw input? Matching your data and your problem to the right paradigm is the first design decision in any machine learning solution.
Answers are worked through in class.

title: Introduction
text:
Types of features
Features in a dataset are either categorical or numerical.

Categorical: non-numeric values, or numeric values with no mathematical meaning. Examples: “Yes”/“No”, customer type (“Regular”, “New”), address.
Numerical: measurable quantities with mathematical meaning. Examples: age, income, transaction amount, square footage.

The values alone are not always enough to determine a feature’s type — context matters. Phone numbers are stored as numbers, but arithmetic on phone numbers is meaningless, so they are categorical. ZIP codes behave the same way. This matters because feature type determines how you process and encode a column.
In the rideshare dataframe:








Feature
Type
Why




cab_type, destination
Categorical
Non-numerical values


distance, price, surge_multiplier
Numerical
Numerical values with meaning


time_stamp
Numerical
Arithmetic on time is meaningful — 2018-12-01 is two days after 2018-11-29

title: Introduction
text:
Exploratory data analysis
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the process of exploring data through plots and descriptive statistics to identify potential relationships and patterns. It comes before any modeling.
Common EDA tasks are examining distributions, visualizing correlations, and detecting outliers. Both lines below assume rides is a pandas dataframe of trips:
rides['distance'].hist()
rides.plot.scatter('distance', 'price')
The histogram shows how one feature is distributed; the scatter plot reveals the relationship between two variables. [CHECK — your speaker notes say the histogram shows “the distribution of prices”, but the code plots distance; I have described it by feature to resolve the mismatch.]
Two popular Python plotting libraries are matplotlib, for static, dynamic and interactive plots, and seaborn, a higher-level library that works especially well with dataframes.
EDA shapes feature selection and preprocessing. It often reveals problems — skewed distributions, missing values, outliers — that must be addressed before modeling. The better you know your data, the better your models will be.

title: Introduction
text:
Classification models
Classification models are supervised models that predict categories or labels from input features.

Examples: logistic regression, naïve Bayes, k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, support vector machines, neural networks.
Use case: predict whether to accept (Yes) or decline (No) an offer.
Output: discrete class labels — Yes and No.

A classification model may predict the class directly, or predict the probability that an instance belongs to a given class. In the probability case, the predicted probability is compared against a threshold to produce a class prediction.
Input features may be categorical or numerical, but the output feature must be categorical.

title: Introduction
text:
Regression models
Regression models are supervised models that predict continuous numerical values.

Examples: linear regression, regression trees, k-NN regression.
Use case: predict the salary attached to an offer.
Output: a real-valued number, for example $70,065.

As with classification, input features may be categorical or numerical, but the output feature should always be numerical.
The distinction from classification is exactly the output type: regression models predict numbers, classification models predict categories.

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised models: clustering
Clustering groups similar observations together without labeled data.

Examples: K-Means clustering, hierarchical clustering.
Use cases: customer segmentation, behavior profiling.
Output: cluster assignments, for example Cluster 1, Cluster 2.

K-Means assigns each instance to one of K groups based on feature similarity. Hierarchical clustering instead builds a tree-like structure of nested clusters. Note what the output is: not a predicted value but a group label.

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised models: outlier detection
Outlier detection identifies rare or unusual instances that do not fit the general pattern.

Example: DBSCAN, which detects outliers as a by-product of clustering.
Use cases: fraud detection (spotting abnormal transactions), error checking (finding data-entry mistakes or system glitches).

No labels are required — the algorithm finds anomalies from the data itself, by comparing each point’s behavior to the others. This is a practical technique when working with real-world, noisy datasets.

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised models: dimension reduction
Dimension reduction simplifies high-dimensional data while keeping important structure.
The most common method is Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which transforms the original features into a smaller number of new, uncorrelated variables called principal components. Think of it as combining features that are strongly related — distance and time, say — into new features that capture the variance.

Data compression: reducing storage or transmission requirements.
Noise reduction: removing irrelevant or redundant features.
Visualization: reducing data to 2D so it can be plotted.

Dimension reduction is often a crucial step before clustering or classification when a dataset has dozens or hundreds of features.

title: Introduction
section: Generalization: the goal of machine learning
text:
Generalization: the goal of machine learning
A model that memorizes its training data can score 100% on it and still be useless.
We do not care how well a model does on data it has seen. We care how well it does on data it has not. That target — performance on unseen data — is called generalization. The test set exists to estimate it: it simulates the future.
This is why data is split into training and test sets before any model is fit, and why a score on training data is never by itself evidence that a model works. [CHECK — my inference from the slide; stated here as a consequence.]

title: Introduction
text:
What is bias?
In machine learning, bias is not a social or ethical term. It refers to error caused by incorrect or overly strong assumptions in the model — the part of the error that persists no matter how much data you collect.
More formally, the error for one instance is the difference between the observed and predicted value:
\[e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]
and the bias is the average error across all predictions:
\[\text{Bias} = \text{mean}(e_i)\]
A model is unbiased when that mean difference is always 0. Least squares regression is a regression model whose weights are estimated so that the bias is guaranteed to be 0.
A model with high bias is too simple to capture the true patterns in the data. It consistently underperforms — this is underfitting. Predicting every ride’s price with a single constant is the extreme case. [CHECK — the reading that this prediction ignores the input entirely, and is therefore systematically wrong however much data you gather, is my elaboration of the slide’s example.]
Bias may come from poor model fitting or violated model assumptions. It may also come from systematic errors in the data itself — underrepresenting a particular group, or failing to measure an important feature.

title: Introduction
text:
What is variance?
Variance measures how much predictions fluctuate across different subsets of the same dataset. Statistically, variance is the average squared difference between an observation and the mean; error variance is the variance of a model’s prediction errors.
A model may perform very well on the training data, but if its predictions change drastically with every new sample, it has high variance. That is overfitting — the model is memorizing noise in the training set instead of learning general patterns. Your model gets all the answers right on one dataset and fails on the next.
A good model has both low bias and low error variance, so its predicted values are consistently close to the observed values.

title: Introduction
text:
The bias–variance trade-off
Bias and variance pull against each other:









Model complexity
Bias
Variance
Result




Simple
High
Low
Underfits — misses patterns, but is stable


Complex
Low
High
Overfits — captures detail, but does not generalize



The goal is the sweet spot: a model complex enough to capture the key relationships, but not so complex that it overreacts to noise.
The archery analogy in the speaker notes is a good way to hold this in mind. Prediction is like trying to hit a bullseye:

Low bias, low error variance: consistently hits the bullseye — the good model.
Low bias, high error variance: occasionally hits the bullseye, but is inconsistent.
High bias, low error variance: consistently hits the same spot, just not the centre.
High bias, high error variance: inaccurate and inconsistent — the worst case.

This is why we split data into training and test sets and watch performance carefully during tuning.

title: Introduction
text:
Training vs. test accuracy
Plotting accuracy against model complexity shows the trade-off directly: training accuracy rises monotonically, while test accuracy rises, peaks, then falls.
The peak of the test curve is the sweet spot — enough model complexity to learn the underlying pattern in the dataset, but not so much that the model starts fitting noise. The widening gap between the two curves past that peak is the visible signature of overfitting. [CHECK — describing the widening gap as the signature of overfitting is my addition; the slide describes the two curves but does not name the gap.]

title: Introduction
section: Knowledge check: reading fit from graphs
text:
Knowledge check: reading fit from graphs
Given the three model graphs on the slides:

Which of the models has the greatest prediction variance?
Which model is most likely to be underfitted?

[CHECK — this paragraph on how to read the graphs is mine.] Read the shape of the fitted line against the data points. A line that stays far from most points is making a strong assumption the data does not support. A line that bends to pass through nearly every point has fit the noise as well as the signal. A line that follows the trend without chasing individual points is balanced.
These visual cues are often more intuitive than the equations, and you will see them again in model diagnostics later in the course.
Answers are worked through in class.

title: Introduction
text:
The six steps
A typical machine learning pipeline includes:

Frame — what is \(x\)? what is \(y\)? what does success mean?
Get & split data — hold some data back.
Preprocess — clean, encode, scale.
Train — fit a model to training data.
Evaluate — metrics on held-out data.
Interpret & act — explain, decide, communicate.

In scikit-learn terms: split the data with train_test_split() to create training and test sets; preprocess features by scaling, encoding, or imputing values; choose a model such as LinearRegression or DecisionTreeClassifier; fit it on the training data; evaluate on the test data using accuracy, mean squared error, or another appropriate metric; then tune and, if warranted, deploy.
This structure is the foundation of everything in this course, and we will refer back to it repeatedly.

title: Introduction
text:
scikit-learn
scikit-learn is a popular Python library for building machine learning models. It is well documented and supports both supervised and unsupervised models, along with preprocessing, training, and evaluation.
The central concept is the estimator: an object that fits a model or algorithm. For example, LinearRegression() trains a linear model. The snippet below assumes X_train and y_train already exist:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
Input and output features are separated into two structures: X and y. Each estimator is initialized into the workspace, with any user-defined settings specified at initialization. Three methods then do the work:







Method
What it does




.fit()
Estimates model parameters, such as regression weights, or applies an algorithm to the input and output features


.predict()
Calculates predicted values for a set of inputs — either new values or the original inputs


.score()
Calculates a performance metric based on the type of machine learning task

Outline

Introduction to machine learning

Here’s how the topic is structured. We’ll start with an introduction to machine learning — what it is. Next, we’ll define features, models, and algorithms — these are the building blocks of any ML system. Then we’ll walk through a practical machine learning workflow using scikit-learn — from loading data to model evaluation. After that, we’ll dive into the bias–variance tradeoff — understanding why models can underfit or overfit. And we’ll wrap up by discussing machine learning ethics — an increasingly important topic in real-world AI deployment.

title: Introduction
text:
What is Machine Learning?

Computers learn patterns from data — no rules written by hand
🗂️ Input: historical data
🔧 Process: learning algorithm
🤖 Output: predictive model


Machine Learning algorithms, perspectives, and real-world application: Empirical evidence from United States trade data (Sakshi Aggarwal, 2023)

So, what exactly is machine learning?
Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence.
It’s focused on building systems that learn patterns from data and make predictions — without being explicitly programmed.
Let’s break that down: The input is historical data — think of spreadsheets, sensor data, images, or text. The process is a learning algorithm — this could be linear regression, decision trees, or a neural network. And the output is a predictive model — a trained function that can make future predictions based on new input data.
Unlike traditional programming, where we write explicit rules, machine learning learns those rules from the data itself.
That’s what makes it so powerful for automation and pattern recognition.
Machine learning uses algorithms and models to make predictions and discover patterns in data.
A model is a mathematical function for describing the relationship between inputs and outputs and making predictions.
An algorithm is a procedure or set of decision rules used to carry out a machine learning task, such as making a prediction.
Machine learning combines tools and theory from computer science, artificial intelligence, statistics, and mathematics to make predictions and apply knowledge to new data.
ML – a subset of AI What’s in AI and not in ML? Areas of knowledge representation, constraint optimization, logical and probabilistic reasoning, and planning. AI is about getting systems to perform tasks that typically require human cognition and decision-making abilities.
FOR NOTES: Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence where computers learn patterns from data and make predictions without being explicitly programmed. 🗂️ Input: Historical data 🔧 Process: Learning algorithm 🤖 Output: Predictive model

text:
ML vs. Traditional Programming

Traditional: Rules + Data → Computer → Answers

You write if "FREE!!!" in subject: spam

Machine learning: Data + Answers → Computer → Rules

You give 10,000 labeled emails; the algorithm produces the rule: the model.

Artificial Intelligence → Machine Learning (this course) → Deep Learning → LLMs
ChatGPT is one member of the family.
This course teaches the family: the concepts every member shares.

In machine learning, a model is a mathematical function that takes input data and maps it to an output.
It makes predictions based on patterns it has learned from the training data.
For example, a linear model might take a feature like distance and use it to predict price, using the formula: y^=fθ(x)=θ0+θ1x = f_(x) = _0 + _1 xy^=fθ(x)=θ0+θ1x Here, xxx is the input feature, yy is the predicted output, and θrepresents the parameters — values the model learns during training.

title: Introduction
text:
What is an Algorithm?
\[\mathcal{A} : (\textit{data},\ \textit{hyperparameters}) \rightarrow f_{\theta^{*}}\]

🗂️ Input: training data and hyperparameters
🔧 Process: optimization rules
🤖 Output: a trained model \(f_{\theta^{*}}\)
Ex: gradient descent trains regression models


Now, while the model is the function that makes predictions, the algorithm is what trains that model.
Think of it like this: the model is the structure, and the algorithm is the recipe for filling in that structure with the right values.
An algorithm takes: Input: training data and hyperparameters Processes: optimization steps, like gradient descent Output: a trained model with the best-fitting parameters
In math terms, we can write this as: A(data,hyperparameters)→fθ∗(, ) f^*_(data,hyperparameters)→fθ∗
For instance, SGDRegressor() in scikit-learn uses stochastic gradient descent to train a model. It updates the model’s weights gradually as it sees each data point. So again — the algorithm is the process, and the model is the result.
FOR NOTES: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure used to train a model on data. Examples: gradient descent algorithms are used to train regression models. It takes: 🔧 Processes: optimization rules

title: Introduction
text:
Model vs Algorithm

🤖 Model: a mathematical function that makes predictions
⚙️ Algorithm: a method that adjusts the model’s parameters using data
📌 These terms are sometimes used interchangeably in casual conversation.


Let’s pause and clarify this distinction:
A model is the mathematical function that makes predictions. Once trained, it can be reused over and over to predict outcomes.
An algorithm is the method used to train the model. It iteratively adjusts the model’s parameters to reduce error.
This distinction is subtle but really important, especially when we start talking about training, optimization, and deployment.

title: Introduction
text:
Example: Predicting Rideshare Price
Goal: Predict the price of a ride using input features.

Machine Learning (zyBooks, 2025)

Let’s walk through a practical example of a machine learning system.
Suppose we want to predict the price of a rideshare trip.
Our input features might include: Distance Starting location Traffic conditions Time of day Vehicle type
We feed these into a model, and it outputs the predicted price.
This is a classic example of supervised learning — we’re using labeled training data where the correct price is already known, so the model can learn from it.
Later, the model can predict the price for a new trip based on similar features.
The price of a ride using a rideshare company like Uber or Lyft can be predicted with machine learning. Inputs like distance, starting location, traffic conditions, time, and vehicle type are recorded for each trip. Inputs are passed into a machine learning model, which uses an algorithm or statistical model to predict the price. The predicted price is the machine learning model’s output.

Now that we’ve talked about models and algorithms, let’s look at the data they learn from.
A dataset is a structured collection of data that typically consists of features and instances.
A feature is a measurable property — for example, the trip’s distance or price. These form the columns of the dataset.
An instance is a single data point — for example, one rideshare trip. These are the rows of the dataset.
When the data is organized in a table — like in a spreadsheet or a pandas dataframe — it’s called tabular data.
This format is extremely common and will be the type we use for most of our examples.
Dataframes store data in tabular format: Each row contains a single instance and each column contains a single feature. Features in the ride share dataframe include distance, cab type, time stamp, destination, price, and adjustment for high demand (surge multiplier). Each instance represents a single rideshare trip.

title: Introduction
text:
Input and Output Features

Inputs (predictors, \(\mathbf{X}\)): what you know
Output (target, response, \(\mathbf{y}\)): what you want to find out
Ex: distance → model → price


Machine Learning (zyBooks, 2025)

In machine learning, we divide features into inputs and outputs. Input features (also called predictors or explanatory variables) are the known information we feed into the model. The output feature (also called the target or response variable) is what we want the model to predict.
In our rideshare example: Input: distance Output: price
You can think of it like this: Inputs = what you know Output = what you want to find out
Choosing the right input features is critical for building accurate models.
FOR NOTES: Inputs (predictors, \(\mathbf{X}\)): Variables used to make a prediction Output (target, response, \(\mathbf{y}\)): The value we want the model to predict Task: Predict ride price based on distance Input feature: distance → model → output feature: price 📌 Think of inputs as “what you know”, and outputs as “what you want to find out.”

title: Introduction
text:
Types of Machine Learning

Supervised — data has labels → Regression (predict a number) · Classification (predict a category)
Unsupervised — no labels, find structure → Clustering (group similar rows) · Dimension reduction (compress columns)
Reinforcement — learn from rewards


Let’s now take a step back and look at the big picture of machine learning types.
There are several learning paradigms, and choosing the right one depends on your task and the type of data you have.
First, we have Supervised Learning. This is when we train the model using labeled data — that is, we already know the correct answers. We use it for tasks like regression and classification.
Next is Unsupervised Learning, where we don’t have labeled outcomes. The model’s goal is to find patterns or structure — for example, clustering similar items together or reducing dimensionality.
Then there’s Reinforcement Learning, which is different — here, the model learns by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback in the form of rewards or penalties. This is used in areas like robotics or game-playing agents.
Later, we’ll also cover semi-supervised and self-supervised learning — two increasingly important techniques in modern ML.
The type of machine learning used depends on the machine learning task. Predicting the price of a rideshare trip based on distance and time is a supervised learning task, since the output feature (price) is known. Categorizing customers as “commuters”, “sports fans”, or “tourists” is unsupervised learning, since these categories are not an observed feature. Adjusting the price of a rideshare after a customer has declined is reinforcement learning. The prediction is updated based on the customer’s decision.
FOR NOTES: no labels: find structure

title: Introduction
text:
Supervised Learning

Learns from labeled data: inputs and correct outputs
Regression → numbers, e.g., ride price $17.32
Classification → categories, e.g., cat vs. dog
📌 Numeric output = regression; categorical = classification


Supervised Learning: Types and Techniques (Bot Pengiun, 2024)

Let’s zoom in on supervised learning, which is the most common ML approach.
In supervised learning, we give the model a set of input features and the correct output — it learns the relationship between the two.
There are two major categories: Regression: This is when we predict numeric values. For example, predicting the price of a ride: $17.32. Classification: This is when we predict categories or labels. For example, classifying an animal as a cat or a dog.
A quick way to distinguish the two: If the output is a number, it’s regression. If the output is a label or class, it’s classification.
We’ll use supervised learning in many of our hands-on examples this semester.
FOR NOTES: Models learn from labeled data — we give them both inputs and correct outputs. Regression: Predict numbers Ex: Predict ride price (e.g., $17.32) Classification: Predict categories Ex: Predict animal type: Cat vs. Dog 📌 If the output is numeric, it’s regression. If it’s categorical, it’s classification.

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised Learning

Finds structure in unlabeled data — no output labels
Clustering: commuters, sports fans, tourists
Outlier detection: rides with abnormally high prices
Dimensionality reduction: transforming data, e.g., PCA


Machine Learning (zyBooks, 2025)

Next is unsupervised learning — and this works without labeled data.
The model is given a dataset and asked to discover structure or relationships within it.
Common unsupervised learning tasks include: Clustering: Grouping instances into meaningful clusters — for example, rideshare customers who behave similarly. Outlier Detection: Identifying unusual or suspicious instances — like a ride that’s far too expensive. Dimensionality Reduction: Transforming a dataset with many features into fewer ones — for example, combining time and distance into a ‘trip intensity’ metric.
This is especially useful for exploratory data analysis or when labels are unavailable.
FOR NOTES: Models find structure in unlabeled data — no output labels provided. Clustering: Group rides into “commuters”, “sports fans”, “tourists” Outlier Detection: Find suspicious rides with abnormally high prices Dimensionality Reduction: Transforming data (e.g., PCA)

title: Introduction
text:
Reinforcement Learning

Learns by trial and error: take actions, receive feedback
Agent: the decision-maker
Environment: where it operates
Reward: feedback after an action
Ex: a self-driving car earns rewards for staying in its lane




Reinforcement Learning: Teaching Computers to Make Optimal Decisions (Bala Priya C, 2023)
Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow (Aurélien Géron, 2019)


Now let’s look at reinforcement learning, which is different from the others.
In reinforcement learning, a model — called an agent — interacts with an environment, takes actions, and learns from rewards or penalties it receives.
Think of a self-driving car learning to stay in its lane. It receives positive feedback (rewards) when it does well — like staying centered. It receives negative feedback (penalties) when it makes mistakes — like crossing a lane.
Key components: The agent makes decisions The environment provides feedback The reward is the signal used to improve over time
This type of learning is often used in robotics, game AI, and recommendation systems.
FOR NOTES: Models learn by trial and error — they take actions and receive feedback. Ex: A self-driving car earns rewards for staying in its lane Key terms: Agent: The decision-maker Environment: Where it operates Reward: Feedback after an action

title: Introduction
text:
Semi-Supervised Learning

Small labeled set + large unlabeled pool
Ex: 100 rides priced, 10,000 not


Semi-Supervised Learning Explained: Techniques and Real-World Applications (Roman Panarin, 2024)

Now we get into more nuanced learning strategies — starting with semi-supervised learning.
This approach uses a small amount of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data.
Why do this? Because labeling data can be expensive and time-consuming, but there’s usually lots of unlabeled data available.
Here’s an example: Suppose you have 100 ride records with labeled prices and 10,000 rides without prices. You train your model on the small labeled set, and then it begins to generalize by learning from the larger unlabeled set.
Semi-supervised learning is widely used in domains like medical imaging and natural language processing, where labeled data is rare but unlabeled data is abundant
Since labeling data is usually time-consuming and costly, you will often have plenty of unlabeled instances, and few labeled instances.
Some algorithms can deal with data that’s partially labeled.
FOR NOTES: Combines a small amount of labeled data with a large pool of unlabeled data. Ex: Only 100 images of rides have prices labeled, but 10,000 don’t. The model starts with labeled data, then generalizes by learning from the rest. Ex: Only 100 images of rides have prices labeled, but 10,000 don’t. The model starts with labeled data, then generalizes by learning from the rest.

title: Introduction
text:
Self-Supervised Learning

Creates its own labels from unlabeled data
📘 NLP: mask a word, train the model to guess it
📷 Vision: predict the missing part of an image




Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow (Aurélien Géron, 2019)
Self Supervised Representation Learning in NLP (Amit Chaudhary, 2020)


Next, we have self-supervised learning, which is one of the most exciting developments in modern machine learning.
In self-supervised learning, the model is trained without any human-labeled data — instead, it generates its own labels from the input data.
For example, in natural language processing: You take a sentence and mask a word: ‘The cab arrived at the ___.’ The model learns to predict the missing word — like ‘airport’ — using the surrounding context.
In computer vision, you might cut out part of an image and ask the model to predict what’s missing.
Self-supervised learning is behind the success of large language models like ChatGPT, BERT, and DALL·E.
It’s incredibly powerful because it lets us learn from vast amounts of raw data, without manual annotation.
FOR NOTES: Learns from unlabeled data by creating its own labels 📘 In NLP, mask a word in a sentence and train the model to guess it: 📷 In vision: Train a model to predict the missing part of an image

Machine Learning (zyBooks, 2025)

Now let’s look at feature types, which are incredibly important in machine learning.
Features generally fall into two categories: Categorical Features: These are variables that represent categories or groups. They may be strings like ‘Regular’ or ‘New’, or numbers with no inherent order — like ZIP codes. Example: Yes/No values, Customer type
Numerical Features: These are measurable values where arithmetic operations make sense. Example: Age, income, transaction amount
One important note: just because a feature is stored as a number doesn’t mean it’s numerical in a mathematical sense. For example, ZIP codes are typically treated as categorical, because there’s no real arithmetic relationship between them. Knowing which features are which affects how we process and encode them.
Feature types Features in a dataset may be categorical or numerical. A categorical feature has non-numerical values, or numerical values without mathematical meaning. Ex: Yes/no, address, type of customer (regular, occasional, new). A numerical feature has numerical values with mathematical meaning. Ex: Amount spent on a transaction, square footage of a house. The actual values in a dataframe may not be enough to determine a feature’s type—context matters. Ex: Phone numbers are numerical, but mathematical operations on phone numbers have no meaning. Thus, phone numbers are categorical features.
Features in the rideshare dataframe can be classified as categorical or numerical. Categorical features have non-numerical values, such as cab type and destination. Numerical features have numerical values with meaning, such as distance, price, and surge multiplier. Time stamp is a numerical feature, since mathematical operations on time have meaning. Ex: 2018-12-01 is two days after 2018-11-29.
FOR NOTES: categorical / numerical (column labels on the source table) Categorical: Non-numeric or no inherent order – e.g., “Yes”/ “No”, Customer Type (“Regular”, “New”) Numerical: Measurable quantities with mathematical meaning – e.g., Age, Income, Transaction amount Categorical: Non-numeric or no inherent order – e.g., “Yes”/ “No”, Customer Type (“Regular”, “New”)

title: Introduction
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis

Explore patterns with graphs and summary statistics
Distributions · correlations · outliers

rides['distance'].hist()
rides.plot.scatter('distance', 'price')

💡 EDA shapes feature selection and preprocessing



Machine Learning (zyBooks, 2025)

Before we train any model, we must explore the data — and that’s where Exploratory Data Analysis, or EDA, comes in.
EDA helps us: Visualize distributions of data Detect patterns and correlations Spot missing values or outliers
Here are a couple of examples: A histogram like rides[distance’].hist() lets you see the distribution of prices. A scatter plot like rides.plot.scatter(‘distance’, ‘price’) helps reveal relationships between two variables.
EDA is both an art and a science. The better you know your data, the better your models will be. This step often reveals issues — like skewed distributions or missing values — that must be addressed before modeling.
Exploratory data analysis is the process of exploring data via plots and descriptive statistics to identify potential relationships and patterns.
Two popular Python libraries for plotting data are matplotlib and seaborn. matplotlib is a library for creating static, dynamic, and interactive plots. seaborn is a high-level library for creating plots that work especially well with dataframes.
FOR NOTES: Use graphs and summary stats to explore patterns in data Common EDA tasks: Examine distributions, Visualize correlations, Detect outliers 💡 EDA helps shape feature selection and preprocessing strategies.

title: Introduction
text:
Classification Models

Predicts categories from input features
Output: discrete class labels — Yes / No
Ex: accept or decline an offer
Models: logistic regression, naïve Bayes, k-NN, decision trees, SVM, neural nets


Introduction to Decision Trees: Why Should You Use Them? (The 365 Team, 2024)

Let’s now shift into different types of models — starting with classification models.
Classification models are used when the output we want to predict is a category or label.
Here are a few examples: Logistic Regression: A linear model used for binary classification Naïve Bayes: Based on probability and Bayes’ theorem Decision Trees: Tree-like structures that split the data based on feature values
Example use case: We might want to predict whether a user will accept or decline an offer — so the model outputs a class: Yes or No. The key thing to remember is: classification problems deal with discrete outputs.
Classification models are supervised machine learning models that classify instances into a predicted level, or class, of a categorical output feature based on the input features.
Classification models may predict the class directly or the probability an instance belongs to a given class. In the probability case, predicted probabilities are compared against a threshold value to produce a class prediction.
In classification, input features may be categorical or numerical, but output features must be categorical.
FOR NOTES: Predict categories or labels based on input features Examples: Logistic Regression, Naïve Bayes, k-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines, Neural Networks Example use case: Predict whether to accept (Yes) or decline (No) an offer Output: discrete class labels – Yes and No

title: Introduction
text:
Regression Models

Predicts continuous numbers
Output: a real value, e.g., $70,065
Ex: predict the salary of an offer
Models: linear regression, regression trees, k-NN regression


Simple Linear Regression model to predict the Salary based on Years of Experience (Yash Kulkarni, 2023)

Now contrast classification with regression models.
Regression is used when the output is a continuous numeric value.
For example: Predicting someone’s salary based on experience Estimating the price of a rideshare trip
Some common regression models: Linear Regression: Fits a straight line through the data Regression Trees: A variant of decision trees tailored for numeric outputs
The important distinction is that regression models predict numbers, not categories.
Later, we’ll walk through coding examples of both classification and regression using scikit-learn.”
Regression models are supervised learning models that predict the value of a numerical output feature based on the input features.
Ex: Simple linear regression is a regression model, since the predicted values are numerical.
Like classification models, categorical or numerical input features may be used in regression.
However, the output feature for a regression model should always be numerical.
FOR NOTES: Predict continuous numerical values Examples: Linear Regression, Regression Trees, k-NN regression Example use case: Predict the salary of an offer Output: real-valued number (e.g., $70,065)

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised Models – Clustering

Groups similar observations — no labels
Ex: K-Means, hierarchical clustering
Use: customer segmentation, behavior profiling
Output: cluster assignments (Cluster 1, Cluster 2)


What is clustering (Google Machine Learning Education, 2025)

Let’s revisit unsupervised models, starting with clustering.
Clustering algorithms group similar instances together, without any labels.
A popular method is K-Means Clustering: It assigns each instance to one of K groups based on feature similarity. Another is Hierarchical Clustering, which builds a tree-like structure of nested clusters.
Use cases include: Customer segmentation: e.g., grouping rideshare users into commuters, tourists, sports fans Behavior profiling: Identifying usage patterns or lifestyle segments
The output here is not a predicted value but a cluster label — like Group 1, Group 2, and so on.
FOR NOTES: Group similar observations together without labeled data Examples: K-Means clustering Example use cases: Customer segmentation and behavior profiling Output: Cluster assignments (e.g., Cluster 1, Cluster 2)

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised Models – Outlier Detection

Finds rare instances that break the pattern
Ex: DBSCAN
Use: fraud detection, error checking
No labels required — anomalies come from the data itself


Outlier Analysis in Data Mining (Scaler, 2023)

Another important type of unsupervised learning is outlier detection.
These models identify instances that are unusual or rare — meaning they don’t fit the general pattern of the data.
One useful algorithm here is DBSCAN, which can detect outliers as a byproduct of clustering.
Use cases include: Fraud detection: Spotting abnormal transactions Data cleaning: Identifying potential entry errors or system glitches
These models don’t require labeled data — they work by comparing each point’s behavior to others in the dataset. It’s a very practical technique, especially when working with real-world, noisy datasets.”
FOR NOTES: Identify rare or unusual instances that don’t fit the general pattern Example: Example use cases: Error checking No labels required — algorithm finds anomalies from data itself

title: Introduction
text:
Unsupervised Models – Dimension Reduction

Simplifies high-dimensional data, keeps the structure
Ex: PCA — combine distance & time into features capturing variance
Use: compression, noise reduction, 2D visualization


Dimension Reduction (Anna Schaar, 2023)

The third major category of unsupervised models we’ll look at is dimensionality reduction.
This technique is used to transform high-dimensional datasets into simple versions, while preserving as much useful information as possible.
The most common method is PCA — Principal Component Analysis.
PCA transforms the original features into a smaller number of new, uncorrelated variables called principal components.
Think of it like combining features that are strongly related into a single, more informative feature.
Example use cases include: Data compression: Reducing storage or transmission requirements Noise reduction: Removing irrelevant or redundant features Visualization: Reducing data to 2D or 3D so it can be plotted
Dimensionality reduction is often a crucial step before clustering or classification when your dataset has dozens or hundreds of features.
FOR NOTES: Simplify high-dimensional data while keeping important structure Example: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) Combine features (e.g., distance & time) into new features capturing variance Example use cases: Visualization (e.g., reduce to 2D for plotting)

These distinctions matter because even though all of these techniques use unlabeled data, they serve very different purposes.
Knowing which one to use depends on your goal: discover patterns, find anomalies, or simplify data.

title: Introduction
section: Generalization: The Goal of Machine Learning
text:
Generalization: The Goal of Machine Learning

A model that memorizes its training data can score 100% on it and still be useless
What matters is performance on data it has not seen
That target is generalization
The test set estimates it: it simulates the future



FOR NOTES: A model that memorizes its training data can score 100% on it and still be useless. We do not care how well a model does on data it has seen. We care how well it does on data it hasn’t. That target — performance on unseen data — is called generalization. The test set exists to estimate it: it simulates the future.

title: Introduction
text:
What is Bias in ML?

Systematic error from overly strong assumptions
Persists no matter how much data you collect
High bias → too simple → underfits
Ex: predicting every ride’s price with one constant


Predicted vs. Actual (Monolith AI, 2023)

Let’s start with bias.
In machine learning, bias is not a social or ethical term — it refers to error caused by incorrect assumptions in the model.
More formally: The error for one instance is: ei=yi−y^ie_i = y_i - _iei=yi−y^i
The bias is the average error across all predictions: Bias=mean(ei) = (e_i)Bias=mean(ei)
A model with high bias is too simple to capture the true patterns in the data. It consistently underperforms — this is called underfitting. Example: using a constant value to predict ride prices would lead to large, systematic errors — regardless of the input.
A model without bias is unbiased — the mean difference between the predicted value and observed value is always 0.
Ex: Least squares regression is a regression model in which the weights are estimated such that the bias is guaranteed to be 0.
Bias may result from poor model fitting or violated model assumptions.
Underlying systematic errors in the data, such as underrepresenting a particular group or failing to measure an important feature, may also result in bias.
FOR NOTES: Bias is a systematic error from overly strong assumptions The part of the error that persists no matter how much data you collect High bias → model too simple → underfits. Example: predicting every ride’s price with a single constant.

title: Introduction
text:
What is Variance in ML?

How much predictions fluctuate across subsets of the same data
High variance → too complex → overfits
Right on one dataset, wrong on the next



Bias-variance decomposition for classification and regression losses (mlxtend)

Now let’s look at the other side of the coin: variance.
Variance refers to how much a model’s predictions fluctuate when trained on different datasets.
You might have a model that performs really well on the training data — but if it changes drastically with every new sample, it has high variance.
This is often a sign of overfitting — the model is memorizing the noise in the training set instead of learning general patterns.
So to recap: High bias = model is too simple → underfitting High variance = model is too complex → overfitting
Our goal is to strike a balance between these two.
Variance is the average squared difference between an observation and the mean.
Error variance is the variance of a model’s prediction errors.
Models with low bias and low error variance have predicted values that are consistently close to the observed values. A good model should have low bias and low error variance.
FOR NOTES: Variance measures how much predictions fluctuate across different subsets of the same dataset. High variance means model is too complex, thus, overfits training data Your model gets all answers right on one dataset but fails on new ones.

title: Introduction
text:
Bias-variance Trade-off

Simple models: high bias, low variance
Complex models: low bias, high variance
Goal: the sweet spot — best generalization



Bias–variance tradeoff (Wikipedia, 2025)

So how do bias and variance interact?
There’s a trade-off: Simple models tend to have high bias but low variance — they miss patterns but are stable Complex models have low bias but high variance — they capture detail but might not generalize
Your job as an ML practitioner is to find the sweet spot: A model that’s complex enough to capture key relationships But not so complex that it overreacts to noise
This is why we split data into training and test sets, and why we monitor model performance carefully during tuning.
Understanding this tradeoff helps you choose appropriate models, adjust their complexity, and improve generalization.
Archery target diagram: High bias: off-center grouping High variance: scattered shots Balanced: tight grouping near center
Prediction is like attempting to hit a bullseye on a target. A good model consistently (low error variance) hits the bullseye (low bias). A model with low bias and high error variance occasionally hits the bullseye but is less consistent. A model with high bias and low error variance consistently hits the same spot on the target, just not the center. The worst case scenario is a model with high bias and high error variance. Models with high bias and error variance are inaccurate and inconsistent.
FOR NOTES: High bias, Low variance Low bias, High variance Goal: Find the sweet spot where both are balanced for best generalization.

The goal is to find the sweet spot: enough model complexity to learn the underlying pattern in the dataset.

Knowledge Check

Which model has the greatest prediction variance?
Which model is most likely underfitted?




Machine Learning (zyBooks, 2025)

Let’s apply what we just learned with a visual knowledge check.
Take a look at the three models shown in the graphs. Each one represents a different kind of fit: Model A shows a straight line far from most points — that’s underfitting, or high bias. Model B fits the data well and generalizes — that’s the ideal fit. Model C is too wiggly, hugging every data point — this is overfitting, or high variance. These visual cues are often more intuitive than equations, and you’ll see them again in diagnostics later in the course. Understanding this trade-off helps you recognize when your model is doing too little or too much.

title: Introduction
text:
Machine Learning Workflow

Frame — what is x? what is y? what is success?
Get & split data — hold some data back
Preprocess — clean, encode, scale
Train — fit a model to training data
Evaluate — metrics on held-out data
Interpret & act — explain, decide, communicate


Here’s what a typical machine learning workflow looks like using scikit-learn.
Step by step: Load and split the data — using train_test_split() to create training and test sets Preprocess features — scale, encode, or impute values as needed Choose a model — such as LinearRegression or DecisionTreeClassifier Fit the model on the training data Evaluate on the test data — using accuracy, mean squared error, etc. Tune and deploy — improve performance, then move it into production if needed
This structure will be the foundation of everything we do in this course — we’ll refer back to this workflow again and again.
Input and output features are separated into two dataframes: X and y. Each estimator is loaded, or initialized, into the Python workspace. Any user-defined settings are specified during initialization. The .fit() method estimates model parameters, such as regression weights, or applies an algorithm to the input and output features. The .predict() method calculates predicted values for a set of inputs, either new values or the original inputs. The .score() method calculates a performance metric based on the type of machine learning task.
FOR NOTES: A typical ML pipeline includes: (lead-in line from the source slide) what is x? what is y? what does success mean? Fit a model to training data

Introduction to scikit-learn

Python library for building ML models
Key concept: an estimator fits a model or algorithm

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

Covers supervised + unsupervised models, preprocessing, training, evaluation


Scikit-learn

To build machine learning models in Python, we’ll be using scikit-learn — one of the most widely used ML libraries.
It’s easy to learn, well-documented, and great for building both supervised and unsupervised models.
A central concept in scikit-learn is the estimator: An estimator is any object that can fit a model to data. For example, LinearRegression() is an estimator used to fit a simple regression model. In code, we use .fit() to train the model:
scikit-learn also includes tools for: Preprocessing data Splitting datasets Evaluating model performance
We’ll use all of these components in the workflow you’re about to see.
FOR NOTES: scikit-learn is a popular Python library for building ML models. Key concept: Estimator — an object that fits a model or algorithm. Ex: LinearRegression() trains a linear model. scikit-learn supports: Supervised + Unsupervised models, Preprocessing, Training, Evaluation. An object that fits a model or algorithm

title: Introduction
text:
Summary – Key Takeaways

Machine learning learns patterns from data to make predictions or discover structure.
The learning approach depends on the data, labels, and task.
Successful models must perform well on unseen data, not just training data.


Let’s wrap up with a quick summary of what we’ve covered today.
You should now be able to: Define key ML terms: dataset, features, models, algorithms Distinguish among the main learning types: Supervised → labeled data Unsupervised → unlabeled data Semi- and self-supervised → mix or auto-generated labels Reinforcement learning → reward-based learning Implement an ML workflow using scikit-learn — from loading data to evaluating models Explain the bias–variance tradeoff and recognize underfitting vs. overfitting Apply the W3C’s 10 ethical principles to guide responsible ML system design These foundational ideas will carry through the rest of the course — from labs and projects to your final assessment.
Core ML Vocabulary You can now speak the language of machine learning: datasets hold the raw observations; features are the measurable attributes; labels/targets are the truths we aim to predict; a model is the mathematical function fθf_{}fθ we train; an algorithm is the procedure that tunes θ; and the training / test split lets us judge how well the model generalizes. Four Learning Paradigms You can distinguish when to use Supervised learning (labeled data, e.g., image classification), Unsupervised learning (no labels, e.g., customer clustering), Semi- / Self-supervised learning (leveraging unlabeled data, e.g., masked-token language models), and Reinforcement learning (agents learn by reward, e.g., game-playing AIs). End-to-End ML Workflow in scikit-learn Starting with a CSV, you can now: train_test_split → preprocessing.Pipeline → model.fit → metrics.evaluate. This pipeline mindset structures every future project—from data ingestion and feature engineering to model tuning and evaluation. Ethical Design Principles Fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability are not add-ons—they shape model choices, data collection, and deployment strategies. You should now be able to identify at least one concrete design or policy decision that supports each principle.
